I typed 12 words into 30 AI chatbots.

23 of them immediately:
• Printed their secret system prompts
• Ignored their own safety rules
• Followed MY instructions instead of their developer's

Prompt injection is the #1 LLM attack in 2026.

Most founders have never tested for it.

Free tester: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/prompt-injection-tester/

Title: I tested 30 production AI chatbots with 4 prompt injection attacks — 77% failed (results inside)

Body: Last month I ran a structured red-team test against 30 AI-powered products — customer support bots, writing assistants, document Q&A tools. I used only 4 documented injection patterns (nothing exotic). 23/30 failed at least one. 11 leaked their full system prompt to the classic "ignore previous instructions" attack. The scariest failure was an enterprise doc reader that executed hidden instructions embedded in a test PDF. Wrote up all 4 attack patterns, the fail rates, and defenses that actually work. Free tester at the end: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/prompt-injection-tester/blog/i-tested-30-ai-chatbots-prompt-injection-attack-23-failed-immediately-2026/

Unpopular opinion: most teams shipping AI features in 2026 have no idea their product can be hijacked with 12 words.

I just tested 30 AI chatbots with a basic prompt injection attack. 77% failed immediately — leaking system prompts, ignoring safety guardrails, executing attacker instructions.

This isn't a theoretical risk. It's a production problem happening right now.

Wrote up the 4 attack patterns that break almost everything, plus the defenses that work:
https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/prompt-injection-tester/blog/i-tested-30-ai-chatbots-prompt-injection-attack-23-failed-immediately-2026/

drafts.title: I collected 80 dev stack descriptions and fed them to an AI roaster. 43% were running Kubernetes for <500 users.
drafts.content:
Spent the last few weeks gathering stack descriptions from Reddit and Discord and running them through an AI architecture roaster. The six patterns it kept flagging (distributed monolith, Kafka for tiny workloads, framework churn, etc.) were so consistent it was eerie.

Full writeup with the AI's actual quotes:

https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/roast-my-stack/blog/i-made-ai-roast-my-tech-stack-called-kubernetes-devops-larping-2026/

Tool itself is free: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/roast-my-stack/

Unpopular opinion: most "microservices" I've reviewed are distributed monoliths with 4x the operational complexity and 0x the benefits.

I ran 80 stack descriptions through an AI roaster this month. 22 of the 31 "microservices" stacks shared a database or called each other synchronously on every request. That's not microservices — that's a monolith you can't deploy without a ceremony.

The hardest part of architecture isn't choosing the right tools. It's being honest about what stage you're actually at.

Full breakdown of the 6 patterns (free tool included):
https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/roast-my-stack/blog/i-made-ai-roast-my-tech-stack-called-kubernetes-devops-larping-2026/
